title: Working on a branch
objectives: Create a branch, switch to it and commit there
Explain why a branch is a pointer to a commit, not a copy of the folder

screens.prose: Your backtest project has three commits. Each circle is a commit. Each solid arrow points from a commit to its **parent**, the commit it was built on. The labels main and HEAD point too, with dashed arrows.

This is the newest commit, the one main points at.
c4 is built on c3, the latest commit, so c4's arrow points to c3.

feedback.correct: c4 is built on c3, so its arrow points back to c3.

byKey.HEAD: HEAD is a label, not a commit. Tap a circle named with a c.

```sh

Switched to a new branch 'experiment'
```

Watch the picture.

screens.prose:
A new idea, in a second project. You make a branch for it, then commit your first change:

```sh
$ git branch momentum
$ git commit -am "Add momentum signal"
```

params.aria: Commit graph: circles are commits, arrows point to parents, labels point at commits

enter.caption: c4 is drawn in. The labels are shown as they were before.

screens.question: Tap the commit main points to now.

hints.text: Did `git branch momentum` move HEAD?
Before the commands, HEAD pointed here. Nothing told it to move.
`git branch` only makes a label. HEAD stays on main, so the commit moves main to c4.

feedback.correct: main moved to c4. The commit landed on main, not on momentum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which branch HEAD was on when you committed.

byKey.switched: You expected the commit to land on momentum. `git branch momentum` only made a label; HEAD stayed on main, so main moved to c4.
byKey.main: That is a label. Tap the commit main points to.
byKey.HEAD: That is a label. Tap a commit.
byKey.c2: Nothing points at c2. Ask which branch HEAD was on when you committed.

explain.text: `git branch momentum` made a label at c3 and left HEAD on main. So your commit moved main to c4, and momentum is still at c3. `git switch -c momentum` makes the label and moves HEAD in one step.

canvas.caption: The commit went to main by accident

screens.prose:
Each command you used makes a label or moves one:

```sh
$ git switch -c experiment   # new branch, HEAD on it
$ git switch main            # HEAD moves; folder follows
$ git branch momentum        # new label; HEAD stays
$ git branch                 # list; * marks HEAD
```

A commit moves the branch HEAD is on, and nothing else.
screens.question: `git branch` prints `experiment`, `* main` and `momentum`, one per line. Which label does your next commit move?

options.why: You took the first name listed. The list is alphabetical; the star marks the branch HEAD is on.
momentum may be the newest branch, but making a branch does not put you on it.
A commit moves one label: the branch HEAD points at.

hints.text: What does the star mean?
The star marks the branch HEAD is on. A commit moves that branch.

feedback.correct: The star marks main, so the commit moves main.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the star.

explain.text: The star in `git branch` marks the branch HEAD points at. Your next commit moves that branch and no other. Run `git branch` before you commit whenever you are unsure.

screens.prose: Your backtest on main produced `results-2026-09.md`: Sharpe 1.12 after costs. You want to try a volatility filter. Afterwards, main must still reproduce that note exactly.
screens.question: Put the commands in order.

lines.text: `git status`, which says On branch main

hints.text: Where must you be before the filter is committed?
Check you are on main, branch off, commit the filter there, go back to main, then rerun.

feedback.correct: The filter lives on vol-filter, and main still makes the same note.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The filter commit has to happen on the new branch.

byKey.commit: You committed before making the branch, so the filter landed on main. Make and switch to the branch first.
byKey.main: You switched back before committing. Your edits would come with you, uncommitted, onto main.
byKey.run: You ran the backtest before going back to main, so it tested the filtered version.
byKey.branch: You can branch first, but check where you are before you start. `git status` comes first.

explain.text: `git switch -c` moves HEAD to vol-filter before the commit, so the filter never touches main. Switching back rewrites the folder to main's commit. That is why the rerun gives Sharpe 1.12 again.

ideas: Each commit points to its parent. A branch is a name pointing at one commit, and HEAD points at the branch you are on.
A commit moves only the branch HEAD is on. A branch contains every commit you reach by following arrows back from it.
`git switch -c name` makes a branch and moves HEAD to it; `git branch name` only makes the label.

formula.name: Make a branch and work on it
formula.note: Check with `git branch`: the star marks where your next commit goes.

summary.trap: `git branch momentum` does not move you onto momentum. Commit straight after it and the commit lands on main.

quiz.prose: main points at c3, the third commit, and HEAD points at main. You run `git switch -c fast-ma`, then commit twice.
quiz.question: How many commits does main contain now?

feedback.correct: main still holds c1, c2 and c3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only fast-ma moved with the two commits.

byKey.counted-branch: You counted the two new commits. They moved fast-ma, the branch HEAD was on, not main.
byKey.tip-only: main points at one commit but contains every commit behind it: c1, c2 and c3.

explain.text: `git switch -c fast-ma` put HEAD on fast-ma, so both commits moved fast-ma. main still points at c3. Following arrows back from c3 gives three commits.

quiz.prose:
You are on main. You type:

```sh
$ git branch test-costs
$ git commit -am "Raise cost to 8 bps"
```
quiz.question: Which branch did the commit move?

options.why: You expected `git branch` to switch you. It only makes the label; HEAD stays on main.
A commit moves one label, the branch HEAD points at.
Committing works on any branch. It moved main.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Did `git branch` move HEAD?

explain.text: `git branch test-costs` made a label and left HEAD on main. So the commit moved main forward. `git switch -c test-costs` would have moved HEAD too.

quiz.prose: Your project folder holds 3 GB of tick data. You run `git switch -c big-test`.
quiz.question: What does git write to disk for the new branch?

options.text: One tiny file holding a commit id
A 3 GB copy of the folder
options.why: You pictured a branch as a copy of the folder. It is a name for one commit.

options.text: A copy of the files you have changed
options.why: Nothing has changed yet. The branch is only a name for the commit you are on.

options.text: A new commit with the current files
options.why: Making a branch makes no commit. It labels the commit you already have.

feedback.correct: A branch is a 41-byte file naming one commit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what a branch is.

explain.text: The branch is one small file holding the id of the commit you are on. No data is copied and no commit is made. That is why branches are cheap enough to make for every idea.

quiz.prose: On experiment you committed carry.py. You run `git switch main`, and carry.py disappears from your folder.
quiz.question: What brings carry.py back into the folder?

options.why: Committed work is kept. Switching only changed which commit the folder shows.
A commit on main saves main's files. carry.py is in experiment's commits.
There is no second folder. A branch is a label, not a copy.

feedback.correct: Switching back makes the folder match experiment again.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where does carry.py live?

explain.text: carry.py lives in a commit that experiment reaches. Switching to experiment makes the folder match that commit again. The file was never lost.
